title: 8. Stage 2 Technical Structure, Institutional Flow & Momentum Setup

epigraph.quote: The trend is your friend until it bends.
epigraph.author: Market maxim

web_blocks.html: Before the chart, a word about dates. The benchmark index had no verified final bar for 13 November when I built the ledger, so this report's verified session is 12 November, when SoftTech closed at ₹420.95. The TradingView read used below was taken after the 13 November session. It shows a last price of ₹425.90 and a volume of only 816 shares for that day, which I treat as provisional [41][42]. Moving averages, RSI and pivot levels are TradingView's. The weekly-average slope, volume tallies and liquidity figures are my own calculations from NSE daily closes [42].

Start with the stage. Stan Weinstein's four-stage framework asks one question first: where is the price relative to its 30-week average, and which way is that average pointing? Our pipeline's rule engine classifies SoftTech as Stage 4 with a timing posture of AVOID_STAGE4_OR_BROKEN and a technical gate of CAP_REJECTED, which forbids any new-capital buy label [41]. I checked the slope the rule does not. The 30-week average is ₹431.16 and it has been rising: it was about ₹392 seven weeks ago and is roughly 15% higher than ten weeks ago [42]. The price, at ₹425.90, is 1.2% below it. A classic Stage 4 has price under a falling average. What I see instead is a stock that doubled from its March low, ran into a volume climax in September and is now pulling back through its short averages while the long ones are still rising. That is closer to a late Stage 2 or early Stage 3 pause. The two systems in our own pipeline also disagree: the market-facts ledger, built from the 50- and 200-day averages at the verified 12 November close, labels the same chart Stage 3 (Topping / Pullback), which matches my reading better than Stage 4 does. None of this changes the answer: the stricter rule controls entries, and valuation already says no.

The averages tell the same story in numbers. The price is below the 10-day average of ₹435.96, the 20-day of ₹431.10 and the 50-day of ₹451.06, and below the weekly 10-week EMA of ₹437.58. It is above the 200-day average of ₹387.28 by 10% and above the weekly 40-week EMA of ₹409.36 by 4% [41]. The 200-day average has risen about 3% in the last twenty sessions and the stock has closed above it on each of the last 60 sessions [42]. Short-term supply has the upper hand; the long-term trend has not been damaged.

Momentum is neutral to soft. Daily RSI is 44.9, weekly RSI 50.6 and four-hour RSI 46.9, none of them oversold or overbought. The 14-day average true range, the typical daily travel, is ₹27.16, which is 6.4% of the price and tells you how wide a stop must be to survive an ordinary day. The Bollinger band width of 12.5% says volatility is not squeezed, so there is no tight volatility-contraction pattern to buy. TradingView's summary rating is -0.27 overall, with -0.53 from the moving averages and 0.00 from the oscillators, which is a lean to the sell side without conviction [41].

Volume is where this stock is most honest. On 11 September SoftTech closed at ₹452.40 on 7,424 shares, 2.3 times its July to early-September average of about 3,250. Over the next five sessions it ran to ₹525.70 on 18 September, a day when 35,070 shares traded, 10.8 times the average and about ₹1.8 crore of turnover [42]. By this stock's standards that is real demand. It was also the climax: the price fell 7.5% within four sessions and has given back 20% since. Across the last 50 sessions, shares traded on up days total 139,270 and on down days 140,521, a ratio of 0.99. There is neither quiet accumulation nor visible distribution, only a stock waiting for its next reason to move.

Relative strength is mixed. Over 252 sessions SoftTech is up 17.2% while the Nifty 50 is down 1.8%, so on a one-year view it is a leader. Over 126 sessions it is down 3.7% against a Nifty gain of 8.2%, and over 63 sessions down 0.5% against a gain of 3.4% [42]. A leader that stopped leading three to six months ago is usually consolidating, and consolidations resolve either way.

Liquidity matters more here than for almost any stock you hold. Average daily turnover is about ₹20 lakh over 30 sessions, ₹21 lakh over 90 and ₹23.5 lakh over 250, with a median of ₹12 lakh and an average of 4,510 shares a day [42]. Your net worth in the positions ledger is ₹42.92 lakh. A 5% position is ₹2.15 lakh, or 504 shares, 11.2% of an average day's volume; a 2% position is about 201 shares, 4.5%. You could get in. Getting out in a hurry on a bad day, in a stock that moved more than 5% in 15 of the last 250 sessions, would cost you more than the stop suggests. Foreign investors hold 0.00% and there is no large institutional holder to provide a floor [37].

The levels you can actually see are these. The October to early-November range ran from ₹412 to ₹462 on closes. Overhead, the 50-day average at ₹451 and the first pivot resistance at ₹471.30 come before the 52-week high of ₹545 and the second pivot at ₹528.15. Below, the 30-week average and 20-day average near ₹431 are the first shelf, the 200-day average at ₹387 the second, and the first pivot support at ₹378.75 the third. The pipeline's rule places a reference support band at ₹373.07-₹384.43 and an invalidation level at ₹365.17 [41]. Treat those as measuring sticks for risk and reward, not as a buy zone. Chapter 9 uses them to show why even a pullback to that band does not pay.

Multi-timeframe, the picture is a dislocation at a major shelf that has not yet been repaired. On the weekly chart the price sits just under a rising 30-week average and above the 40-week EMA, with weekly RSI at 50.6. On the daily chart it is under the 20- and 50-day averages and above the 200-day. On the four-hour chart it is under both the 20-period EMA of ₹431.01 and the 50-period SMA of ₹433.19, with RSI at 46.9 [41]. The options-desk script describes the four-hour chart as turning up and above its EMA20. With the price at ₹425.90 and the EMA20 at ₹431.01 that sentence does not match the numbers, so I do not rely on it. The four-hour chart has not turned. The test of repair would be a close back above ₹431 and then ₹451 on volume well above 4,500 shares.

Is there a short-term trading edge? No, and for four independent reasons. The timing gate is CAP_REJECTED. Volume shows balance rather than accumulation. The stock's liquidity makes tactical entry and exit expensive. And Chapter 7 shows that the price, not just the timing, is the problem. If you want a short list of what would improve the chart: a higher low above ₹412, a close above ₹451 on twice the usual volume, and a weekly close above ₹462 that reclaims the whole October range. Even then the valuation gate in Chapter 9 would still say no.

Options give you no alternative route. SoftTech is not in the NSE futures and options segment, so the options desk records NOT_OPTIONABLE_OR_ILLIQUID and the only way to express a view is the cash share [41]. The Robinhood session check applies only to the US market and was not applicable here, and no TradingView browser tab was open, so the multi-timeframe read comes from TradingView's public data rather than a logged-in session.

The technical ledger below the chart mixes two dated sources, and you should read it that way. The close, 20-day, 50-day and 200-day averages, RSI and ATR in its first rows come from the market-facts ledger at the verified 12 November close (₹420.95, RSI 43.0, ATR ₹27.61, 50-day ₹450.37). The weekly averages, pivots, ratings and extension percentages come from TradingView's read after the 13 November session, which is why this chapter's text, quoting TradingView, shows ₹425.90, RSI 44.9 and a 50-day average of ₹451.06. The differences are small and none changes a conclusion. My own calculations from NSE closes (slopes, volume tallies, turnover) are labelled as such.

The sizing table is deliberately empty. The pipeline's tier for a rejected setup carries a risk budget of zero basis points, so the risk-adjusted weight is 0%. That is the rule working as designed: when the decision is not to own the stock, the answer to how much is nothing, and the levels in the table are reference values for the next review, not orders.

Then I would look at the volume bars on the right. There is a tall spike in mid-September and nothing remarkable since. That tells me the buyers who wanted the stock in September have had their turn, and the next group has not arrived. I would not call it broken. I would call it undecided.

Liquidity is easier to feel than to calculate. Picture a theatre with a door that lets only a few hundred people out each day. In a calm week nobody notices. On the evening everybody wants to leave at once, the door is the whole story. When this stock trades about 4,500 shares a day and you own 500, you are one-ninth of the crowd at the door. That is the reason the stop in a thin stock is a promise your broker may not be able to keep.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: A chart answers one question: who is in control right now. Here the long-term buyers still hold the weekly trend and short-term sellers hold the daily one. When two groups disagree, price usually goes sideways until one of them runs out of patience. Your job is not to guess which. It is to avoid paying a premium price while the argument continues.
